chunks: Spectrum of sharp vs slow-edged square waves. The question: How does the frequency content of sharp vs not sharp square waves?
A spectrum is the list of sine waves that add up to a signal, with how strong each one is. Two square waves with the same repeat rate share the same main sine wave.
If one has sharp edges and the other has slow edges, they differ in the high-frequency part. The slow-edged wave has much less of it.
Think of the bass and treble knobs on a stereo. The repeat rate sets the bass, the deep main note, and it stays put. The edge sharpness is the treble knob.
Sharp edges turn the treble all the way up. Slow edges turn it down, so the sound is mellower but the bass is unchanged. The cut is gradual, though, not a sudden wall.
Same period and swing; only the ramp changes. At t r equals 0. 25T the flat top shrinks to a quarter of the period and the corners are strongly rounded.
A trapezoid with t r equals 0. 5T would be a triangle.
Spectrum: the recipe of sine waves that build a signal ("Spectrum of a square wave and pulse train"). Harmonic: a sine wave at a whole-number multiple of the repeat rate.
Rise time: how long an edge takes. A longer rise time means a slower edge. Knee frequency: the frequency where the high harmonics start dropping faster.
It is about 1 / (π times rise time) for a straight-line edge. dB: a way to compare strengths. 20 decibels less means 10 times smaller voltage.
Take a 100 megahertz clock. Its harmonics sit at 100, 300, 500 megahertz and so on. Give one version 100 picoseconds edges and another 1 nanoseconds edges.
The knees are near 3 gigahertz and 300 megahertz. Below about 300 megahertz the two spectra look almost the same. Above it, the 1 nanoseconds version's harmonics fall away faster.
Far above both knees, the 10 times slower edge has 10 times weaker harmonics, which is 20 decibels less.
That is the whole idea: slowing the edge leaves the low harmonics alone and trims the high ones.
"Sharp and slow-edged square waves share the same fundamental and low harmonics. The sharp one falls at 20 decibels per decade, one over n, all the way up.

The slow-edged one follows that until a knee near one over pi times the rise time, then falls at 40 decibels per decade because of the extra sinc factor, and it has nulls at multiples of one over the rise time.
So high-frequency energy scales inversely with rise time: a 10 times slower edge is 20 decibels quieter up high, at the cost of timing margin."
